perfectionism.title: Perfectionism: When the pursuit of perfection becomes a trap
perfectionism.description: Perfectionism is a drive for excellence that can be both an ally and an enemy. In this article, we’ll explore unhelpful perfectionism—the kind that leads to self-criticism, fear of making mistakes, and, ultimately, depression.

texts: Perfectionism can unexpectedly act as both a symptom and a cause of depression.

For many, high standards and strict demands on themselves and others feel like a driving force. However, when expectations become unrealistic, they can turn into a trap, leading to a constant sense of inadequacy, relentless self-criticism, and, eventually, depression.
“Perfectionism” means striving for the ideal. It takes various forms:

Self-oriented perfectionism is characterized by an internal drive for perfection. People with this trait might spend sleepless nights rechecking reports for errors, refuse to leave the house because their hair isn’t neat enough, feel deep guilt over the smallest slips, and constantly feel like they aren’t good enough.
Other-oriented perfectionism involves demanding perfection from others—such as parents expecting straight A’s from their children, or a manager requiring flawless work from their employees.

To understand if you’re struggling with unhelpful perfectionism, look for signs such as an unrelenting need for perfection, dependency on others’ opinions, fear of disappointing people, striving for unreachable goals, an inability to accept criticism, and being overly harsh with yourself and others.
<q author="Leo Tolstoy">If you seek perfection, you will never be satisfied.</q>
If you recognize yourself in these descriptions, don’t lose hope. There are effective ways to work through perfectionism.
However, it is important to realize that at the very heart of perfectionism lies a paradox: perfection is an illusion.
In this world, everything can be improved, and the pursuit of absolute perfection is destined to end in disappointment.

<important>Realizing this can be the first step toward breaking free from the shackles of perfectionism, allowing you to focus on achieving realistic goals and learning to find joy in the imperfection of the world and yourself.</important>
To work through something, you must first clearly recognize the need to do so.
If you believe perfectionism is helpful and see nothing wrong with it, it will be difficult to make any changes.
Let’s start by looking at the pros and cons of perfectionism.
It certainly has positive aspects; for example, high standards can encourage hard work. However, when faced with mistakes, you might become overly self-critical.
There is a difference between adaptive and unhelpful perfectionism.
Adaptive perfectionism can strengthen your persistence and responsibility, helping you reach your goals without unnecessary self-criticism or fear of making mistakes.
At the same time, unhelpful perfectionism leads to excessive demands on yourself and others, and constant worry over every mistake, which can trigger anxiety, depression, and procrastination.
The line between these two types is very thin.

test.question: What is the type of perfectionism that does not lead to self-criticism and fear of mistakes?

texts: Try making a list of the pros and cons of your perfectionism. It might look something like this:
Pros:
• I pay attention to detail
• I have a high level of responsibility
• It helps me achieve good results at work
Cons:
• I am very afraid of making mistakes and always criticize myself for them
• I get so tense and nervous that I often can’t work well
• I am so critical of myself that it’s hard to simply enjoy life
• I can’t truly relax at home because I’m always finding something to do

If your analysis shows that perfectionism is negatively affecting your life and you feel the need to work on it, we’re ready to share effective tips and techniques to help you overcome this challenge.

plan.title: Technique: Action Plan Against Procrastination
plan.description: In this article, we’ll reveal the secrets to effectively tackling procrastination using the proven anti-procrastination sheet method. Discover how simple steps—like breaking down tasks and realistically assessing their difficulty and potential enjoyment—can transform your approach to work and personal life, leading to increased productivity and improved mental well-being.

texts: This technique may be particularly helpful if you tend to put things off because they feel too difficult or unrewarding.
In the first stage, write one or two tasks you’ve been procrastinating on in one column.
If a task requires significant time and effort, it’s best to break it down into several small steps, each taking no more than 15–20 minutes.
Next, in the second column, use a scale from 0 to 100% to rate how difficult you think completing the task will be.
<important>If a task seems easy, give it a low rating—for example, 10% or 20%. If it seems more difficult, a rating of 80% or 90% would be appropriate.</important>
In the third column, also using a percentage scale, record your prediction of how much enjoyment completing the task will bring.
Only start working on the task after you have written down your predictions.
<q author="Jack London">You cannot wait for inspiration. You must go out and meet it with work.</q>
Once finished, use the last two columns to record how difficult the task actually was and how much enjoyment you experienced from completing it or from the result, using a percentage scale.
Example:
A lawyer who recently lost their job couldn’t start looking for a new one because the process of preparing a resume and the job search itself felt like insurmountable tasks.
To start, the task “find a job” should be broken down into several steps so it doesn’t feel overwhelming and doesn’t trigger procrastination:
• Sit down and write a resume.
• Review it with fresh eyes the next day and make adjustments.
• Dedicate 10–15 minutes daily to monitoring job search sites.
• Write a cover or motivational letter.
• Send the resume to selected vacancies, tailoring the cover letter to the specific role and company.
In this way, you can make a large task feel more manageable by breaking it into small steps.
Then, rate each task by difficulty and predicted enjoyment. An example might look like this:
• Task: Write a resume
• Predicted difficulty: 80%
• Predicted enjoyment: 15%
• Actual difficulty: 30%
• Actual enjoyment: 70%
As you can see, writing the resume turned out to be much easier and more enjoyable than expected.

Surprisingly, the process got moving, and self-esteem and motivation grew significantly thanks to the results achieved. The effect of this technique was so impressive that the lawyer began applying it in other areas of life, significantly increasing both productivity and self-confidence.

read.title: Inside Out: Breaking Free from Mind Reading
read.description: This article explores the cognitive distortion known as “mind reading,” where we tend to assume we know what others are thinking. We’ll look at how this distortion can lead to mistaken perceptions of how others view us, affecting our emotional state and interpersonal relationships. Finally, the article offers ways to overcome this tendency—such as building self-awareness and practicing open communication—to improve mutual understanding and mental well-being.

texts: The last cognitive distortion we’ll look at in detail is called “mind reading”.
This is a thinking error where we’re convinced we know what another person is thinking about us, often assuming they’re thinking something negative.
If we rely too heavily on mind reading, we may misinterpret how others see us, which can seriously impact our mood.
We often make mistakes without even realizing what another person is actually thinking or why they acted the way they did.
This can lead to anxiety, various fears, and sometimes even paranoia. It can also cause conflict, resentment, arguments, and, of course, depression.
<q author="Viktor Frankl">We cannot change the situations life presents to us, but we can change our ability to experience them.</q>
Examples:
• I won’t tell her about my struggles because she’ll think I’m weak
• He definitely won’t like my work because I’m not happy with it myself
• She’s looking at me so strangely; she must think I’m fat
Of course, in all these examples, there is a slight possibility that people might actually think that way, be dissatisfied, or see you as weak.

But that probability is much lower than it seems. We can read people’s facial expressions and gestures, but that doesn’t mean someone giving us a sideways glance is necessarily thinking something bad about us.
We mistake our own thoughts for the truth and start acting based on them, rather than on the actual likelihood of other possibilities.
Here are a few ways to work with “mind reading”:
Awareness
Start noticing these kinds of thoughts and ask yourself: “Can I really read other people’s minds?”
Obviously, you can’t. To prove this to yourself, you can even run a few experiments. Write down what you think people are thinking about you, and then check it.
You can verify this either through a direct conversation with the person or by observing their actions toward you.
<q author="Anaïs Nin">We do not see things as they are. We see them as we are.</q>
Challenging your thoughts
Ask yourself: “What evidence do I have that supports these thoughts? And what evidence do I have against them?”
This technique will help you formalize and weigh your assumptions.
We don’t usually reason very rationally, but when we weigh the “pros” and “cons,” we’re forced to engage our critical thinking more deeply.
Finding alternatives
Ask yourself: “What else could this person be thinking?”
For those ready to go further, an open and honest conversation can help resolve many misunderstandings.
Instead of struggling with your assumptions, it’s better to ask the person directly.
Don’t assume that cognitive distortions are a sign of serious mental pathology.
They are present in all of us to some degree.

<important>What matters is how often they occur and what we do about them: we can either believe these distorted thoughts 100% and experience negative emotions, or we can question and analyze them, leading to a more accurate and nuanced view of the situation.</important>
Working on cognitive distortions may take time and effort, but it can significantly improve your mental well-being and your relationships with those around you.
